What I Learned Rebuilding My Sourdough Starter From Scratch

Written by Priya Raman · 9 min read

For almost four years my sourdough starter lived in the same jar on the same shelf, fed every morning before the kettle went on. Then I went away for a month, a well-meaning house sitter put it in the fridge without feeding it, and I came home to a grey, sour-smelling puddle that refused to rise no matter what I did.

I tried to revive it three times. Each attempt started well and then collapsed after a few days. Eventually I gave up, washed the jar, and started again with nothing but flour and water. This post is a record of what worked the fourth time, and the mistakes I made along the way.

The routine that worked

  • Equal weights of wholemeal rye flour and lukewarm water for the first five days.
  • Discard all but a tablespoon of starter before every feed.
  • Keep the jar somewhere steady and warm, ideally around twenty-five degrees.
  • Switch to strong white bread flour once it doubles reliably within six hours.

The rye flour made the biggest difference. It is full of the wild yeasts and bacteria you are trying to encourage, and it ferments far more enthusiastically than white flour in the early days. By day four my jar was bubbling in a way it never had during the failed revivals.

Mistakes I would avoid next time

The first mistake was impatience. Around day three most new starters go quiet, because the bacteria that caused the early burst of bubbles die off as the mixture becomes more acidic. I panicked the first time this happened and added a pinch of commercial yeast, which only masked the problem.

The second mistake was using water straight from the tap. Our water is heavily chlorinated, and leaving a jug out overnight before feeding seemed to help noticeably. I cannot prove it made the difference, but it costs nothing to do.

Finally, I stopped worrying about the exact schedule. A feed an hour or two late did no harm at all. What mattered was consistency over weeks, not precision over hours.

The new starter has now been going for six months, and the loaves are, if anything, better than before. If yours has given up on you, do not be afraid to begin again. It only takes a week, a bag of rye flour and a little patience.
